::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
📄 **For the group work:** [download this grid as a PDF](ConflictAnalysis.pdf). The
lecture slides explain where each question comes from; the worked example there is lithium
mining in the Salar de Atacama, Chile.
:::
:::

**Task (20 min, country groups).** Open the [Environmental Justice Atlas](https://ejatlas.org)
and filter by your country. Pick **one** conflict — ideally one linked to a major export of
your country. No case for your country? Take one linked to its main export commodity
(Atlas of Economic Complexity). Work through the seven questions; then report in **2 minutes,
starting with question 7**.

**Why these questions.** They follow the conceptual framework of @scheidel2018 — conflicts
over the environment arise from a growing social metabolism (*why*), are carried by
particular actors (*through whom*), are fought in different valuation languages (*how*),
and unfold in stages of mobilisation (*when*). The sub-questions follow the template on which
every EJAtlas case is coded [@temper2015], so most answers can be found on the case page.

| | Question | Guiding sub-questions | Based on |
|:-:|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------|:---------------|
| **1** | **What and where?** | Which project, which commodity, which type of conflict? Where exactly, since when? | @temper2015 |
| **2** | **Why?** The metabolic driver | Which flow of materials, energy, water or waste is at stake? Where does the commodity go — who consumes it? Who receives the benefits, who bears the costs? | @scheidel2018; @martinezalier2010 |
| **3** | **Through whom?** Actors | Companies (and their home countries), state agencies, financiers; affected and mobilising groups, NGOs. Who has power, money, legal standing? | @scheidel2018; @temper2015 |
| **4** | **Impacts** | Environmental, health and socio-economic impacts. Visible already, or potential? Which groups are hit hardest? | @temper2015; @scheidel2023 |
| **5** | **How?** Valuation languages | In which terms do the parties argue — money, jobs, compensation, or livelihood, territory, sacredness, rights? Are some languages excluded from the decision? | @martinezalier2002; @martinezalier2010 |
| **6** | **When?** Mobilisation and outcome | Preventive, reacting to the project, or demanding reparation? Forms of protest, litigation, intensity. Repression or violence — direct, but also slow or structural? Outcome? | @scheidel2020; @navas2018 |
| **7** | **So what?** For your poster | What does the case tell you about your country's position in world trade — and about the twin challenge of social provisioning and ecological sustainability? | Session 5; @dorninger2021 |

**Read the atlas critically.** The EJAtlas lists conflicts that were *documented*, often
together with those mobilising [@temper2015]. Coverage differs strongly between countries
[@scheidel2023], and a missing entry does not mean there is no conflict. Treat a case page
as a starting point: check it against at least one peer-reviewed case study or another
independent source, and note on your poster where your information comes from.

**Background.** Why the poor often defend the environment — because they live from it — is
the argument of the *environmentalism of the poor* [@martinezalier2002;
@anguelovski2014]. A global overview of what mobilisations achieve and at what risk is
@scheidel2020. The worked example in the lecture draws on @floresfernandez2023 (open access)
and @jerez2021.
